In this world each placement lands 4 columns to the right of the chosen anchor, wrapping around: a brick chosen at column x lands at column (x + 4) mod 8, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There is no evidence yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds, so it never builds a design exactly. At the default recipe the budget is 131k steps in only 32 PPO updates of 4,096 samples, which may simply be too few policy improvements. On the architecture side, a correct placement depends on how the cells under one footprint relate to each other: the brick lands at the highest column under it, so every cell at that layer must be in the target. The current head only sees fixed max, min and average pools over each footprint, plus 5x5 context. This round is a 2x2 test missing one cell: (1) the same network with more, smaller updates and a longer horizon; (2) a new learned footprint-convolution head that also sees the raw observation, with the default recipe; (3) both together. Because the starting score is 0, any reliable non-zero result on 2 seeds counts as progress.

### Round 2
Every trial so far scored 0 on dev, and none built a single design exactly late in training. Neither the recipe change (more, smaller updates) nor the learned footprint-conv head made a difference. So the problem is not tuning. The networks probably cannot express the key rule for each placement: the landing layer is the maximum column height under the footprint, and every footprint cell at that layer must be a missing target cell. Shorter columns must not seal target cells underneath. That rule takes two stages: first pool the heights over the footprint, then check each cell against that pooled layer. One pooling pass or one convolution cannot do this easily. A second untested lever is the amount of data: fewer PPO epochs buy 1.9x to 3.3x more environment steps. This round tests a two-stage landing head, and splits the network effect from the effect of more data.

### Round 3
All six trials scored exactly 0 on dev and 0 in training, on both seeds. That covered three different placement heads, 32 to 128 updates, and 125k to 230k steps. A uniform zero like this points to one blocking cause, not a head that is slightly weak. Two causes are plausible. (1) Every head so far assumes the conv feature at (y, x) belongs to the action anchored at (y, x). If this world indexes actions differently (axes swapped, a different anchor corner, or a permutation), translation-equivariant heads cannot learn at all. A dense head, which can learn any index mapping, tests this. (2) The policy may collapse onto DONE. Random placements mostly fill cells outside the target, so they score below DONE's 0, and an early DONE becomes an attractor. A higher entropy weight and a longer horizon (gamma) test this. Three proposals form a 2x2 test missing one cell: hybrid head alone, entropy recipe alone, and both, each with about 230k steps.

### Round 4
All nine trials scored exactly 0 on dev and 0 on training success in the last 10% of training, for both seeds of every trial. None of these changes moved the result off zero: three head designs (footprint conv, two-stage landing head, dense hybrid), more data with ppo_epochs 2 and about 230k steps, extra entropy, and a longer gamma. So no lever has any evidence behind it yet. Either the task cannot be learned at roughly 200k steps, or the world differs from the description in a way that breaks the footprint-aligned heads, for example in anchor or axis convention. In this last round I test both at once. One network makes no assumption about where a footprint sits relative to its anchor: it uses a 3x3 learned conv per brick type and takes the legal-action mask, reshaped into action layout, as input. The other change gives the most data the budget allows: ppo_epochs 1 for about 360–420k steps. A plain-baseline control with the same recipe separates the two effects.
